question: For the EU’s anti-poverty strategy to succeed, it is essential that poverty and social data at the Member-State level provide a reliable basis for decision-making. Amidst this strategic process, it is particularly concerning that the anomalies identified in the latest Hungarian EUSILC data raise questions about the accuracy of the EU’s statistical system.

Such methodological inconsistencies could not only distort the evaluation of the situation in Hungary, but also jeopardise policy conclusions affecting the EU as a whole. Ensuring the integrity of the statistics is therefore crucial for the strategy’s credibility. For these reasons, I pose the following questions to the Commission: 1.
Can Eurostat confirm the nature of the anomalies identified in the Hungarian EU-SILC data, and provide details on the review process? Will Eurostat make the results of the review public?
How will Eurostat guarantee the accuracy of Hungarian poverty data following the revision, particularly during the preparation period for the EU’s anti-poverty strategy?
Does Eurostat plan to review further data reflecting Hungarian social conditions (e.g. data on energy poverty), given the political sensitivity of these indicators?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.2.2026) The Hungarian Central Statistical Office (HCSO) revised the EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC) data from 2019 to 2024. Eurostat received these data on 16 June 2025, and, following validation, published them on 10 October 2025. A brief note1 explaining the revisions was released at the same time.

The HCSO provided further details on these revisions in Annex 112 of their 2024 quality report3. Eurostat is committed to ensuring the highest quality of European statistics. The EU-SILC data are provided in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2019/1700, supported by methodological guidelines, data validation procedures, and continuous bilateral discussions with national statistical offices.

These quality assurance frameworks and processes enable Eurostat to continuously develop methodologically, validate, and enhance the quality of statistics. National statistical authorities and Eurostat conduct reviews of social data solely based on methodological needs, that is, when data anomalies or potential irregularities require examination with the goal of upholding statistical accuracy.
